title: The Shepherd of Hermas
hookLine: visions of the church as an old woman growing young, from a man once sold in Rome
tomorrow: asked to judge a brother, a desert monk brings a leaking basket. why?

lines: AN OLD WOMAN WITH A BOOK.
cards: Aging filters show a face at eighty in a few seconds: the lines, the gray. Run one backward and the years fall away. An early Christian book of visions runs it backward on purpose.
It opens with a confession: its writer, Hermas, says the man who raised him sold him to a woman named Rhoda, in Rome. Then the visions begin.
An elderly woman in shining clothes sits on a great chair and reads to him from a book. Hermas guesses she must be someone from the old stories. He's wrong.

teach.b: A young man tells him: she is the Church. Why old? Because she was created before all things.
Hermas sees her three times, and each time she's younger: first old and seated, then with a younger face, standing, and at last young and full of joy. Why?

teach.h: HIS SPIRIT WAS THE OLD ONE.
teach.b: She looked old, he's told, because his own spirit was old, worn down by worry and doubt. She grew younger as his spirit was renewed, the way good news lifts someone out of grief.
So her age is read in the faces of the people who see her. A psalm has the same hope: "thy youth is renewed like the eagle's." Sikhs have a cousin of this.
Their congregational prayer, the Ardas, closes by asking that through God's Name their spirits stay in chardi kala, rising spirits, and that by God's will all may fare well.
What's shared: a people's spirit isn't fixed by its age or its troubles; it can rise again, and it's prayed for together.
The honest difference: in Hermas, the one who grows young is the Church, shown in a vision, as one man's hope returns.
In the Ardas, chardi kala is asked through the Name, a Sikh ideal of rising spirits even in hardship, joined to the good of everyone.

how: The Shepherd of Hermas isn't read in Sunday worship today, but Christians study it as one of the early writings after the New Testament, and its pictures turn up in sermons on renewal.

games.q: what does “the shepherd of hermas” mean?
o: a book of visions where the Church grows young
a letter from a shepherd to a church in Rome
a parable of Jesus about a lost sheep and its keeper

games.q: the visions of Hermas — tap the pairs.
p: the Church, created before all things
a Sikh prayer for rising spirits

s: in the vision the Church looks old because she's tired of people
she looked old because Hermas's own spirit was worn down; she grew young as his hope came back.
the book is named for an angel dressed as a shepherd
the shepherd comes in a later vision and gives the book its title.
chardi kala, in the Sikh Ardas, means rising spirits
the Ardas asks for it, along with the good of all.

games.q: your grandfather's men's group at church is down to five, all retired. he says it 'feels old.' what does Hermas's vision suggest about a group that feels old?
o: its age shows in its spirit; hope can make it young again.
it's finished; an old group can't come back.
only new young members can make it young.
games.why: in Hermas, the Church looked old because the one seeing her was worn down, and grew young as his hope returned. her age wasn't counted in years.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind a community you belong to: a church, a family, a team, a circle of friends.
See it first on a worn-out day, then let it grow younger in your mind as hope comes back to one person in it, then another, and stay with that picture.

wordCard.voice: The Shepherd of Hermas. An early Christian book of visions, where the Church appears as a woman who grows young.

orig.note: Greek: shepherd, the word in the book's title.

carryVoice: Here's the line: the church grows young, and in the vision it happens when hope comes back. Until next time.
